title: LLM Pricing Agents as Rote Learners
abstract: Firms are increasingly experimenting with LLM-based agents for pricing decisions. We study the reliability of these decisions and develop, to our knowledge, the first analytically tractable framework that links Transformer pretraining to an LLM agent's pricing decisions. We explicitly characterize the weights learned by a pretrained Transformer and use them to derive the agent's demand-estimation rule, its bias and variance, and the resulting pricing regret. The analysis reveals a fundamental limitation: the agent behaves like a "rote learner." Although it can adapt to a new pricing environment using examples supplied in the prompt, the way it interprets those examples remains anchored to the covariate structure encountered during pretraining. As a result, its demand estimates can be systematically biased when the prompt and pretraining covariate distributions are misaligned. Increasing the number of historical examples in the prompt reduces estimation variance and makes the agent's decisions more stable, but does not remove this bias; more context can therefore make the agent more consistent without making it more accurate. This limitation is particularly critical for commercial LLMs because users typically cannot observe the models' pretraining data and hence cannot verify whether the required alignment holds. Numerical experiments with pretrained Transformers, real-world pricing data, and commercial LLMs including GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Grok provide evidence consistent with these theoretical implications.
why: LLM pricing agents show rote-learner limitation anchored to pretraining

title: Common AI Information and Capital Allocation
abstract: This paper studies how AI progress affects capital allocation through financial information aggregation. Using institutional portfolio holdings, we document that manager pairs with greater common alignment with AI-extractable information subsequently hold more similar portfolios. Motivated by this evidence, we develop a model in which investors choose the quantity and composition of private and AI information, and firms learn from equilibrium asset prices before investing. A shared AI model error survives aggregation and enters prices, and investors may underestimate the overlap between AI information and prices. AI progress therefore changes both investors' information precision and prices' exposure to common errors. Cheaper access initially raises aggregate productivity when high costs keep AI use negligible, but further cost reductions can reverse the gain as AI research displaces private research. Improvements from very low model accuracy can instead lower productivity when increased reliance raises common-error exposure more than informed trading reduces noise-trader contamination. Numerical equilibria trace a J-shaped relationship between model accuracy and TFP. These results show how AI progress can expand investors' information acquisition while reducing the information prices convey to firms, worsening capital allocation even when firms use prices optimally.
why: AI capital allocation model with real data, shows negative productivity effect

title: Endogenous Compliance with Portfolio Regulation
abstract: Regulatory thresholds need not produce the directional trading their statutory language implies, because institutions can change the category governing the portfolio. We study China's 2014 rule defining a stock fund as one holding at least 80% of assets in stocks. Stock-to-hybrid conversions bunch at the transition deadline; all 106 recovered numerical equity-range pairs remain unchanged, although this selected evidence does not certify every contract. Contractual mismatch is associated with 0.615 higher semiannual gross turnover and an independently measured 18.54-basis-point transaction-expense increase during the transition, with net purchases indistinguishable from zero. The turnover preperiod is not flat, and its causal magnitude is sensitive to the largest preperiod differential movement. Separately, a larger capped baseline realized stock-weight shortfall predicts lower quarterly investor flows; it is not a contractual-gap estimate. A partial-equilibrium model describes trade-offs among category flexibility, directional demand, adjustment activity, and risk capacity. Under fixed portfolios and assets, prohibiting reclassification implies a mechanical minimum of RMB 17.25 billion in purchases, not an identified realized saving or welfare ranking. Generative-AI disclosure: OpenAI generative-AI tools and another large language model assisted with data inspection and rebuilding, statistical programming and estimation, manuscript audits, evidence organization, reference checks, document construction, and language editing. OpenAI Codex also assisted with mathematical typesetting for the submission copy. A detailed disclosure appears in the manuscript. The author remains responsible for the manuscript and submitted version.
why: Regulatory compliance microstructure with real trades; China-specific, limits transferability

title: Identifying Monetary Policy Shocks with Large Language Models
abstract: We use large language models to measure sentiment indicators from pre-FOMC briefing materials and construct aggregate-level control variables for Federal Reserve staff expectations about the U.S. economy. Our low-dimensional, AI-based measures extract economically meaningful information from the semantic context of the briefing materials without relying on high-dimensional regularized regressions, thereby avoiding the associated regularization bias. As a complement to the existing narrative approaches, our AI-based monetary policy shocks provide a credible alternative for subsequent impulse response analysis.
why: LLM sentiment from Fed materials; straightforward application

title: Industry Factors in Nasdaq Technology Stock Returns, 2021-2026
abstract: We study the co-movement of 50 Nasdaq-listed technology stocks using 260 weekly dividend-adjusted returns from August 2021 to August 2026. Exploratory factor analysis of returns in excess of the Nasdaq-100, with the number of factors chosen by parallel analysis, identifies eight industry factors that explain 52% of excess-return variance. The solution is robust to oblique rotation and maximum-likelihood extraction (mean Tucker congruence 0.96 and 0.93). The factors are distinct from the Fama-French five factors and momentum: adding them raises the median explained variance of individual stocks from 39% to 58%, a significant gain for 88% of stocks. In a point-in-time universe of 42 Nasdaq-100 technology members as of August 2021, five of the eight factors reappear (congruence 0.88-0.99). The three that do not-AI compute, sentiment-driven growth, and storage and memory-are also the best performers, so part of their outperformance reflects hindsight in stock selection. Out-of-sample tests find no week-ahead predictability in any factor portfolio.
why: Factor analysis robust to methods; tech-sector specific, no ML component

title: AI-Equipped Institutional Investors, XBRL Standardization, and the Reach of Structured-Data Disclosure Mandates
abstract: The Financial Data Transparency Act of 2022 and the SEC's XBRL mandates presume that stand-ardization binds uniformly across filers. I examine the alternative: machine-readability is jointlydetermined with a firm's investor clientele. For U.S.-listed 10-K filers, 2018 to 2026, I measure afirm's machine-reading clientele as the equal-weighted share of its 13F holders whose filings indi-cate AI use. Measurement is itself a finding. The ownership-weighted measure is mechanicallyconfounded with Big-3 ownership and carries no signal; composition measures do. No text-basedrefinement separates AI-specific processing capability from the broader sophistication of a non-index institutional clientele, so the evidence concerns an AI-classified clientele rather than verifiedAI adoption. Firms with larger machine-reading clienteles show lower XBRL custom-tag ratiosafter 2022. The association concentrates among small firms and not-yet-sorted clienteles, survivespredetermined complexity controls, and is absent at pre-treatment placebo dates. It is significantunder conventional clustering and attenuates under randomization and few-cluster-robust infer-ence, reported in full. The evidence excludes strong within-firm adjustment but cannot separatestatic from dynamic sorting. Structured-data mandates bind most where clienteles have not sorted;standardization pressure on small, complex filers is best paired with taxonomy support.
why: Disclosure compliance study; AI measurement confounded with ownership

title: Explainable Machine Learning for U.S. Equity Selection: Integrating Fundamental,Technical, and Sentiment Signals
abstract: The investment management industry increasingly relies on artificial intelligence and machine learning (ML) to process the growing volume of structured and unstructured data available to equity investors. Existing research, however, remains fragmented: studies typically examine fundamental, technical, or sentiment information in isolation, use small samples or complex model ensembles when they attempt integration, and evaluate performance using statistical accuracy rather than economically meaningful, cost-adjusted portfolio outcomes. This paper presents the conceptual foundation, literature synthesis, methodological design, and empirical results for an explainable machine-learning framework, an XGBoost model paired with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) that integrates fundamental, technical, and market-sentiment information to predict forward returns of U.S. equities. Sentiment is operationalized through four established, publicly available market-wide indices rather than security-level text. The design uses walk-forward validation, feature-set ablation, cost-adjusted portfolio backtests, and SHAP based attribution across market regimes. The study produced out-of-sample results (2019–2025; 82 monthly cross-sections) for 504 U.S. large-cap equities show modest predictive power: the integrated model attains a mean monthly rank information coefficient of .026 (HAC t = 1.36, p = .173), and its improvement over a fundamentals-only baseline (.023) is not statistically significant (one-sided p = .428); neither technical nor sentiment features adds significant value after multiplicity adjustment (Holm-adjusted p = 1.00). The integrated top-decile long-only portfolio earns 27.5% annually net of costs (Sharpe ratio 0.88) versus 17.4% (0.79) for the equal weighted universe, but with higher volatility, no significant alpha (4.6% per year, t = 0.99), and a Sharpe advantage reduces at 50 basis points of one-way cost. Portfolios built on fundamental features, alone or with sentiment, are the exception, earning significant alphas versus SPY (9.9%,t = 2.74; 9.1%, t = 2.27). SHAP attribution is spread across fundamental (about 44%), technical (39%), and sentiment (17%) features, led by firm size, beta, and price-trend measures, and feature rankings are largely stable across market regimes (Spearman ρ = .68-.91). The study is grounded in the Adaptive Markets Hypothesis (Lo, 2004) and Shapley-value theory.
why: XGBoost equity model; no baseline, transaction costs, or OOS shown

title: Talking Less About Supply Chain Finance: How U.S. Generative AI Expectations Reshaped Discourse in Chinese Tech Firms
abstract: This paper examines how the rise of U.S.-origin generative AI reshaped corporate discourse on supply chain finance (SCF) in Chinese technology firms, using a keyword-frequency-based SCF disclosure index constructed from annual reports. Because the annual data reveal adjustment before ChatGPT's public launch, we interpret the empirical design as capturing an AI expectation-and-salience window rather than a purely discrete one-day shock. Keeping the reported estimates unchanged, the difference-in-differences results show a significant relative decline in SCF discourse among technology firms. The mechanism evidence is asymmetric: the treatment indicator is positively associated with a financing-process efficiency measure, has no statistically discernible average effect on DEA-based technical or pure technical efficiency, is associated with tighter financing-constraint indices, and raises measured debt costs without a detectable short-run increase in realized accounting volatility. We therefore interpret the results as evidence consistent with strategic narrative reallocation under technological discontinuity, with financing conditions acting as a potential amplifier rather than as a uniquely identified mediation chain. The dynamic analysis further indicates that the discursive response developed gradually through an anticipatory phase before ChatGPT's public release and intensified thereafter. The findings contribute to research on cross-border technology spillovers, managerial attention, and corporate disclosure by showing that frontier technologies can reshape what follower-economy firms emphasize before widespread adoption is complete.
why: Corporate discourse analysis on supply chain finance, not financial ML

title: Exorbitant Inflation: AI Capital Deepening, Dollar Hegemony, and the Erosion of Cash
abstract: This paper argues that the world has entered a regime of structurally higher inflation driven by three mutually reinforcing forces: (i) a reserve-currency hegemon whose public debt now exceeds $40 trillion and is cheapest to service by eroding its real value; (ii) the largest private capital-formation wave since the railways, the AI build-out, which spends roughly $700 billion a year in 2026 on physically scarce inputs; and (iii) a US-China rivalry that turns that spending into a matter of state will rather than market return. The well-known part of the story is that fiat money loses purchasing power over time. The new contribution is the AI Capital Deepening Shock: front-loaded AI investment creates demand today and supply only later, and it collides with inelastic inputs (electricity, memory chips, copper, electricians). Because geopolitics makes this spending price-insensitive, it raises the inflation floor rather than producing a one-off spike. We formalize the argument in a simple debt-dynamics framework, present evidence from official and market sources, and draw one central implication: in this regime, idle cash is the asset most certain to lose, while productive real assets in the hegemon and its allies are the default store of value. We close with the counterarguments that could falsify the thesis.
why: Macro AI theory without empirical data or implementable methods

title: Economic Headroom, Drawdown Capital, and MDCER
abstract: This paper develops a microfounded theory of portfolio choice when drawdown distance changes the marginal economic cost of risk. It defines economic headroom, separates drawdown capital from ordinary risk measures, and derives the marginal drawdown-capital efficiency result (MDCER). The level ratio sometimes used in practice follows under matched homogeneity as a sufficient structural condition; fixed drawdown thresholds generally break that bridge. A finite envelope of smooth law-specific capital functions can be nonsmooth when maximizing laws switch; directional derivatives then replace a universal gradient ratio. The framework yields activation tests, counterexamples, and a disciplined interpretation of marginal attribution without asserting that shadow prices or constraint slack are new. AI-use disclosure: AI tools assisted with manuscript preparation and review. The author reviewed and approved the manuscript and retains responsibility for its content and results.
why: Pure portfolio theory with drawdown dynamics; no data, no implementation

title: Sargent, Williams, and Zha at Twenty Dissecting The Posterior Surface Of The Central Bank Learning Model
abstract: This paper revisits the inuential Sargent, Williams, and Zha (2006) model, which synthesized the "bad luck" and "bad policy" explanations of the 1970s US stagation through the lens of central bank learning. By dissecting the posterior surface of the central bank's static and dynamic Phelps problems, we uncover profound structural degeneracies in the parameter space. To navigate this highly irregular manifold without resorting to forced empirical calibrations, we develop an adaptive Metropolis-Hastingswithin-Gibbs sampler equipped with a real-time Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) machine learning module. Our re-estimation reveals an alternative narrative: the inationary peaks were largely driven by exogenous shocks that triggered "algorithmic panics." These shocks forced the Kalman lter into extreme belief updating, highlighting the vulnerability of adaptive learning mechanisms and demonstrating that the loss of ination control was not purely a deliberate policy choice.
why: Macro central bank learning model; computational MCMC work on old theory

title: The Incompleteness of Accounting as a Technology of Control: Artificial Intelligence, Accounting Legitimation, and the Structural Fractures of Anti-Money Laundering
abstract: This study investigates which structural vulnerability in contemporary accounting most resists efforts to prevent illicit funds from acquiring legitimacy within the economic system. It conceptualises accounting-mediated legitimation (ACCLEG) as the degree to which illicit or economically contested value acquires a formally plausible accounting, documentary, corporate, or financial representation. An exploratory mixed-methods design combines standardised responses from eight large language models, lexical textometry using IRaMuTeQ, documentary analysis of 30 publicly documented financial-crime cases, and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA). Five structural conditions are examined: procedural shielding, beneficial-ownership opacity, data fragmentation, valuation subjectivity, and regulatory rigidity. The documentary evidence shows that procedural shielding and data fragmentation are pervasive, while valuation subjectivity is less frequent but substantially more discriminating. Under the principal fsQCA specification, the intermediate solution is PROC * VAL → ACCLEG, whereas the parsimonious solution reduces to VAL → ACCLEG, with consistency of 0.976 and coverage of 0.617. The results indicate that valuation subjectivity is the core configurational condition associated with high accounting-mediated legitimation, while procedural shielding operates primarily as a contextual condition. The findings extend critical accounting and AML research by showing that the central vulnerability is not always missing information or concealed ownership, but the capacity of formally acceptable representations to confer plausibility on economic value whose substantive basis remains difficult to verify independently. The study interprets this limitation through a restricted Gödelian analogy, conceptualising accounting incompleteness as epistemic and institutional rather than mathematical.
why: Uses LLMs but AML-focused; AI is framing not contribution

title: The 1% Fallacy: Defining a Market Small Enough to Win and Forecasting Growth Through Adoption, Capacity, and Risk
abstract: Entrepreneurs routinely describe large markets as evidence of opportunity and then make a deceptively comforting claim: “we only need 1% of that market to meet our financial projections.” The arithmetic may be correct, but it is not a strategy and rarely constitutes a defensible forecast. This paper argues that startup market analysis must solve two different problems. First, founders must define an initial target market that is large enough to support the intended business yet small enough for a startup to become strategically meaningful—a “big fish in a small pond” rather than an irrelevant participant in an enormous market. Second, founders must distinguish the legitimate target market from the portion of that market that is ready to adopt in the near term and from the volume the startup is internally able and willing to serve. The paper introduces the Boundary Cliff as a conceptual test for legitimate segmentation. A market boundary is stronger when crossing it produces a material decline in customer need, relative value, or likelihood of choosing the product. This distinguishes genuine market segmentation from arbitrary age, geographic, or demographic cutoffs often selected merely to make a market appear smaller. Some boundaries are steep and categorical; others are gradual and require evidence of an economically meaningful threshold. The paper then develops a two-sided constraint-based approach to early growth forecasting. Adoption-limited demand represents the market side: the number of customers in the legitimate target market realistically ready to buy during a given period. Four company-side constraints—sales capacity, delivery capacity, financing capacity, and an intentional risk limit—combine to form an Internal Growth Ceiling. The realistic near-term sales ceiling is the lower of adoption-limited demand and the Internal Growth Ceiling, not an artificially chosen percentage of total addressable market. A historical 2005 Texas Instruments USB 3.0 business-planning case illustrates how analogous technologies and segment-specific adoption drivers can inform forecasts under uncertainty. The paper concludes with implications for founders, educators, and investors and proposes directions for empirical research on market-boundary quality and constraint-based growth forecasting. AI Disclosure: This article was drafted and refined with the assistance of generative AI (ChatGPT). The conceptual framework, structure, arguments, and conclusions are my own and are grounded in my research, teaching, and professional experience. AI was used as a drafting and editing tool.
why: Startup market strategy; off-topic for financial ML/LLM practitioner

title: Consideration: A Lawyer's Field Guide to Money, Markets, and the Rules Underneath Them
abstract: Consideration : A Lawyer's Field Guide to Money, Markets, and the Rules Underneath Them argues that there is no purely financial decision. Every price rests on a rule someone wrote, an agency that interprets it, and a court that will eventually say what it means. The book follows that idea through forty-four chapters in nine parts. It starts with the legal construction of money and banking, then covers the firm as a creature of statute, securities regulation after Chevron, the Uniform Commercial Code, insolvency and antitrust, tax and corporate crime, labor, property, and insurance, and the regulated edges of commerce: gambling, cannabis, licensing, and nonprofits. A coda teaches statutory reading as a working skill. Part IX turns to artificial intelligence. It covers the legal status of AI systems, the copyright fights over training data, model risk in finance, a lawyer's professional duties when a machine drafts, and government use of algorithms. It closes with a three-chapter manual on using these tools in teaching and practice. Every chapter examines its subject in three layers, in the same order: the federal statute, the agency that administers it, and the Illinois overlay. Each one opens with a real case or episode. It then states the governing rule in black letter with verifiable citations, works fact patterns through model CiRAC answers, recovers the history that explains why the rule has its shape, and ends with discussion questions and flashcards. The book is written for lawyers, law and business students, and serious general readers. Its law is stated as of September 2026, and it flags unsettled law as unsettled.
